They swear their most solemn oaths that if the Prophet commanded them to march out, they would certainly go, and the commentary explains the marching as setting out to fight his enemy and the enemy of the believers. The oath is offered as proof of loyalty. What it reveals, however, is a willingness to promise what they had just refused to practise when a judgement was at stake.

phrases.translation: Say, “˹You˺ do not ˹have to˺ swear; your obedience is well known!”
phrases.explanation: The answer dismisses the oath. They are told not to swear, and the commentary explains the phrase as pointing to an obedience that is already known to be untrue, so their swearing adds nothing to a matter that is settled. The command cuts through the performance of loyalty and names it. A promise made to replace action is treated here as an insult rather than a reassurance.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do.”
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with Allah's awareness of what they do, and the commentary explains this as His full knowledge of their conduct, including the oaths and what lies behind them. The reminder moves the matter out of the room where the swearing took place. It also prepares for the command that follows, which turns from what they promised to what they must actually do.

phrases.translation: Say, “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.
phrases.explanation: The command is given in the simplest terms, and it is addressed to the same people and to the rest of the community. Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and the commentary notes that obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah. Everything the passage has discussed about accepting judgement comes down to this one instruction. The verse does not argue further but states the duty and then explains what follows if it is refused.

phrases.translation: But if you turn away, then he is only responsible for his duty and you are responsible for yours.
phrases.explanation: The refusal is then addressed. If you turn away, the Messenger bears only what he was charged with and you bear what was laid on you, and the commentary explains the messenger's charge as delivering the message and the people's as following him. Responsibility is divided so that nobody can shift it onto someone else. The verse also confirms that the messenger may not be blamed for a refusal he could not prevent.

phrases.translation: And if you obey him, you will be ˹rightly˺ guided.
phrases.explanation: A condition is then attached to obedience. If you obey him, you will be rightly guided, and the commentary explains this as following the right path and finding the truth in one's affairs. Guidance is presented as the fruit of obedience rather than its precondition, which reverses the attitude of the hypocrites who wanted to see the outcome before committing. The verse makes the command an offer as well as a duty.

phrases.translation: The Messenger’s duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly.”
phrases.explanation: The verse closes by restating the limit of the messenger's role. His duty is only to deliver the message clearly, and the commentary explains this as conveying what Allah intends in a way that makes it plain, leaving obedience as the people's own responsibility. If they obey, they profit, and if they refuse, they harm themselves. The sentence defines the messenger's task so that no failure of response can be blamed on an unclear delivery.

phrases.translation: Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good
phrases.explanation: The verse opens with a promise made to a specific group. Allah has promised those among the addressees who believe and do good, and the commentary explains the good deeds as obeying Allah and His Messenger in what they were commanded and forbidden. Belief and action are named together, so the promise is not attached to a profession alone. The wording places the promise in the middle of a passage about obedience being tested.

phrases.translation: that He will certainly make them successors in the land, as He did with those before them;
phrases.explanation: The content of the promise is succession in the land. The commentary explains this as Allah causing them to inherit the land of those who associated others with Him, among Arabs and non-Arabs, and making them kings and rulers over it. It also explains the comparison with those before them by the children of Israel, who were given the land after the tyrants were destroyed. The promise is therefore historical as well as future.

phrases.translation: and will surely establish for them their faith which He has chosen for them;
phrases.explanation: The promise continues with the establishment of their religion. Allah will entrench the faith He has chosen for them, and the commentary explains this as establishing and strengthening the way of life He approved for them and commanded them to follow. The gift is not only territory but security for a way of living. What is promised is that the religion will be able to stand in public rather than survive in hiding.

phrases.translation: and will indeed change their fear into security—˹provided that˺ they worship Me, associating nothing with Me.
phrases.explanation: The last element is the exchange of fear for safety. Allah will change their fear into security, and the commentary explains the change as a transformation of state while the people remain the same, which is why the doubled form of the verb is preferred. The condition attached is worship of Allah alone, with nothing associated with Him. The promise is thus tied to the very thing the surah has been demanding throughout.

phrases.translation: But whoever disbelieves after this ˹promise˺,
phrases.explanation: A warning is then attached. Whoever disbelieves after this promise, it is they who will be the rebellious, and the commentary explains the word as leaving the obedience that has just been described. The verse keeps the promise from being read as a guarantee that no longer depends on anything. A gift that is conditioned on worship can be lost by the same conduct that forfeits any trust.

phrases.translation: it is they who will be the rebellious
phrases.explanation: The verse ends by naming those who would fall away, and the commentary treats the description as a departure from the command rather than a single act of doubt. Set beside the promise of succession, warning, and safety, the phrase is sobering, since it imagines people who received all of that and then turned back. The surah has already shown what happens to a community that treats its covenant lightly.

phrases.translation: Moreover, establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and obey the Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The command is direct and practical. Establish prayer, pay the alms-tax, and obey the Messenger, and the commentary explains the first as performing the prayer within its proper limits without letting it lapse, the second as giving the obligatory alms to those entitled to it, and the third as following the Messenger in what he commanded and forbade. The three together describe the ordinary shape of a faithful life.

phrases.translation: so you may be shown mercy
phrases.explanation: The purpose is then named. So you may be shown mercy, and the commentary explains this as asking that Allah show them mercy and thereby save them from His punishment. The commands are not presented as a price paid for mercy but as the path along which mercy is met. After the promise and the warning of the previous verse, the surah offers a plain and repeatable way to live.

phrases.translation: Do not think ˹O Prophet˺ that the disbelievers can escape in the land.
phrases.explanation: The verse addresses a possible miscalculation. The Prophet is told not to suppose that those who disbelieve can escape in the land, and the commentary explains the phrase as their being unable to elude Allah's power when He wills to destroy them. Delay is not escape. The enemies of the message had outlived earlier warnings and might have thought themselves safe, and the verse names that impression as a mistake.

phrases.translation: The Fire will be their home.
phrases.explanation: The fire is then named as their refuge, and the commentary explains the abode as what awaits them after destruction. The word used suggests a place one returns to, which is a grim reversal for people who thought the world was their home. Having been told that they cannot escape, the reader is now told where they will be found instead.

phrases.translation: Indeed, what an evil destination
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with an exclamation of disapproval. What an evil destination, and the commentary explains it as the worst conceivable end. The sentence is short and leaves nothing to add, since the destination has already been named. It also balances the promise of succession given to the believers a few verses earlier, so that the two ends of obedience and denial are set side by side.

phrases.translation: O believers! Let those ˹bondspeople˺ in your possession and those of you who are still under age ask for your permission ˹to come in˺ at three times:
phrases.explanation: Household privacy is now given a rule with fixed hours. Slaves and children who have not reached maturity must ask permission at three specific times, and the commentary explains that the command covers male and female slaves without distinction. The rule is not about entering the house in general but about entering at moments when the household is not prepared. It applies to the people who move most freely inside a home.

phrases.translation: before dawn prayer, when you take off your ˹outer˺ clothes at noon, and after the late evening prayer.
phrases.explanation: The three times are then named. They are before the dawn prayer, at noon when clothes are taken off, and after the late evening prayer, and the commentary explains these as the moments when people lay aside their garments and rest. Nothing exotic is being regulated, only the ordinary daily rhythm of a household. The times chosen are the ones in which a person expects not to be seen.

phrases.translation: ˹These are˺ three times of privacy for you.
phrases.explanation: The verse then names what these moments are. They are three times of privacy for the household, and the commentary explains the word as referring to the exposure of the body that people avoid. Calling them times of privacy rather than times of restriction keeps the focus on the dignity being protected. The rule protects the household's own modesty rather than merely limiting the servants' movement.

phrases.translation: Other than these times, there is no blame on you or them to move freely, attending to one another.
phrases.explanation: The rest of the day is left unrestricted. Other than these times there is no blame on you or them to move about and attend to one another, and the commentary explains this as free movement for service and company outside those moments. The verse avoids turning a limited protection into a permanent barrier. Households must still function, and the command is calibrated to the few moments that actually require it.

phrases.translation: This is how Allah makes the revelations clear to you,
phrases.explanation: The passage closes with the reminder that these are Allah's clarifications. This is how Allah makes the revelations clear to you, and the commentary treats the phrase as marking a complete and understandable instruction rather than an arbitrary one. The rules about privacy, like the earlier rules about entering houses, are presented as part of a body of guidance. The reader is meant to see coherence rather than a list of restrictions.

phrases.translation: for Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with the two names that accompany the instruction. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise, knowing the needs of a household and ordering the command accordingly. The pairing answers the two doubts a reader might have, whether the rule fits real life and whether it is arbitrary. The closing formula appears repeatedly in this surah, marking each block of commands as considered guidance.

phrases.translation: And when your children reach the age of puberty, let them seek permission ˹to come in˺,
phrases.explanation: The rule for children is then raised to a higher level. When they reach the age of puberty they must ask permission, and the commentary explains that they may no longer enter at any time without it, neither during the three times already named nor afterwards. Childhood had required permission only at those hours, but adulthood removes the exemption entirely. The verse marks the moment when a household's youngest members become subject to the general rule.

phrases.translation: as their seniors do.
phrases.explanation: The standard is set by those who have gone before them, and the commentary explains this as the adults among a man's sons and free relatives who already asked permission. The new rule is therefore not new at all but the entry of the young into an existing practice. It also gives the maturing child a clear example to follow rather than an unexplained restriction.

phrases.translation: This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you,
phrases.explanation: The verse repeats the formula that has closed the previous instructions. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, and the commentary treats the phrase as marking a complete and intelligible command. Its return here shows that the rules about privacy, servants, children, and guests form one connected body of guidance. The reader is being trained to see them as a single discipline of modesty.

phrases.translation: for Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with the two names that have accompanied each of these commands. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise, so the rule fits the stages of a person's life and the needs of a household. The pair also answers the complaint that such instructions are intrusive, since the One who gives them knows how homes actually work. The command is presented as ordered rather than arbitrary.

phrases.translation: As for elderly women past the age of marriage,
phrases.explanation: The verse makes an allowance for elderly women who are past the age of marriage. The commentary explains the group as women who have ceased childbearing because of old age, who no longer menstruate and no longer bear children. The description matters, since the concession rests on a change in their situation rather than on their own preference. The verse names the condition precisely before stating what is permitted.

phrases.translation: there is no blame on them if they take off their ˹outer˺ garments,
phrases.explanation: The permission is to lay aside outer garments, and the commentary explains these as the wrap worn over the head covering and the mantle worn over the clothing. It adds that this applies among close male relatives and also before unrelated men, which shows how far the concession reaches. Removing a layer is treated as a small relief for women for whom the reason behind the covering has changed.

phrases.translation: without revealing their adornments.
phrases.explanation: A condition is attached. They may not do this in order to display their adornment, and the commentary explains such display as a woman showing beauties that should be concealed. The allowance is thus about comfort rather than appearance. The distinction is important, since the same act can be a relief in one intention and a provocation in another, and the verse names the intention.

phrases.translation: But it is better for them if they avoid this ˹altogether˺.
phrases.explanation: The verse then prefers restraint even where permission exists. It is better for them if they avoid it altogether, and the commentary explains this as continuing to wear the wrap and the mantle. What is permitted is not thereby recommended. The sentence gives the allowance without encouraging it, which is characteristic of the surah's manner of setting a limit and then pointing to what is better within it.

phrases.translation: And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with Allah as All-Hearing and All-Knowing. The commentary applies the names to what is said and intended in such a matter, where the difference between comfort and display lies in the heart. Since the ruling depends on intention, the two names supply the knowledge that no community can provide. The verse ends by reminding the reader that the concession is not a licence to be careless.

phrases.translation: There is no restriction on the blind, or the disabled, or the sick.
phrases.explanation: The verse removes a barrier that had grown up around eating. There is no restriction on the blind, the disabled, or the sick, and the commentary reports that some people had refused to eat with them or to let them eat in others' houses, and that the verse came down to lift that. The concern was not the food but the company, and the verse names the people who had been made to feel unwelcome.

phrases.translation: Nor on yourselves if you eat from your homes, or the homes of your fathers, or your mothers, or your brothers, or your sisters, or your paternal uncles, or your paternal aunts, or your maternal uncles, or your maternal aunts, or from the homes in your trust, or ˹the homes of˺ your friends.
phrases.explanation: The permission then extends to a long list of houses. A person may eat in his own home, or those of his father, mother, brothers, sisters, paternal and maternal uncles and aunts, homes entrusted to him, or those of his friends. The list covers the circle within which people actually moved and ate. The commentary reports the fear that had arisen about eating food belonging to someone else, and the verse answers it by naming the relationships in which such eating is blameless.

phrases.translation: There is no blame on you eating together or separately.
phrases.explanation: The verse also settles a smaller social anxiety. There is no blame in eating together or separately, and the commentary explains the permission as lifting a burden people had placed on themselves about eating in company or alone. Meals are not a test of piety. The sentence has the effect of removing awkwardness from ordinary hospitality, so that nobody is embarrassed by how many share the dish.

phrases.translation: However, when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting ˹of peace˺ from Allah, blessed and good.
phrases.explanation: The command about entering houses is then restated in its positive form. When you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting of peace from Allah, blessed and good, and the commentary explains it as the greeting of peace being given and returned among those present. Having earlier required permission before entry, the verse now supplies the words that belong at the door. The greeting is described as from Allah, so courtesy becomes worship.

phrases.translation: This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand
phrases.explanation: The passage closes with the familiar formula. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand, and the commentary treats the phrase as marking the completeness of what has been explained. The section has dealt with privacy, greetings, and eating, and the closing words gather them as one body of guidance. Understanding is named as the aim, since these rules make sense once a person sees the whole.

phrases.translation: The ˹true˺ believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The verse defines the believers by what they do in a gathering. They believe in Allah and His Messenger, and the commentary explains belief here as sincere affirmation rather than a claim. The definition is deliberately narrow, since it is about to identify those who do not leave without permission. Faith is being described at the point where it becomes visible in conduct.

phrases.translation: and when they are with him on a public matter, they do not leave without his permission.
phrases.explanation: The specific conduct is then named. When they are with him on a public matter, they do not leave without his permission, and the commentary explains the public matter as anything that gathers them, whether a battle, a prayer, or a consultation. The rule concerns attendance on the Prophet himself and the respect owed to a leader. Leaving without permission would break the gathering and the trust that holds it together.

phrases.translation: Indeed, those who ask your permission ˹O Prophet˺ are the ones who ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and His Messenger.
phrases.explanation: The verse then draws the line between believers and the rest. Those who ask permission are the ones who truly believe in Allah and His Messenger, and the commentary explains this as a contrast with those who leave without asking, in disobedience to Allah and His Messenger. The point is not that asking permission creates faith but that faith shows itself in such obedience. The test is small and ordinary, which is what makes it revealing.

phrases.translation: So when they ask your permission for a private matter, grant permission to whoever you wish and ask Allah’s forgiveness for them.
phrases.explanation: A concession is then given for personal need. When they ask permission for a private matter, permission may be granted to whoever is chosen, and the commentary explains the private matter as a need that has befallen the person. The leader is not required to refuse or to grant indiscriminately, since the decision is left to him. The rule holds the discipline in place while allowing for the ordinary business of a life.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with an instruction to pray for those who ask. Ask Allah's forgiveness for them, and the commentary explains this as calling on Allah to show mercy and forgive what lies between the person and his Lord. Permission granted is accompanied by prayer rather than by suspicion. The two names at the end, All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, show the spirit in which a leader should respond to those who ask.

phrases.translation: Do not treat the Messenger’s summons to you ˹as lightly˺ as your summons to one another.
phrases.explanation: The command concerns how the Messenger's call is treated. Believers must not regard his summons as they regard a call from one of themselves, and the commentary records two readings of the verse. One is that they must not provoke his invocation against them, since his prayer against someone strikes. The other is that they must not address him roughly but with gentleness and respect. Both readings keep the same concern, that he is not an equal to be treated casually.

phrases.translation: Allah certainly knows those of you who slip away, hiding behind others.
phrases.explanation: The verse then turns to those who slip out of the gathering. Allah certainly knows those who slip away, hiding behind others, and the commentary explains the image as people concealing themselves behind one another and then leaving without permission. The behaviour is furtive by nature, which is why it is described in this way. It also shows that the earlier command was being evaded quietly rather than openly.

phrases.translation: So let those who disobey his orders beware, for an affliction may befall them, or a painful torment may overtake them
phrases.explanation: The warning is then stated in two forms. Those who disobey his orders should beware, for an affliction may befall them or a painful torment may overtake them, and the commentary explains the affliction as a trial that could reach the heart and seal it, while the torment is the punishment that follows. The verse does not treat the matter as a breach of etiquette. Leaving without permission is placed among the things that can damage a person's faith.

phrases.translation: Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: The surah closes by returning to ownership. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and the commentary draws the practical conclusion that a possession ought not to disobey its owner or defy Him. The argument is quiet but firm, since the command about leaving a gathering is set within the larger fact of belonging. What people owe the Messenger is part of what they owe the One who sent him.

phrases.translation: He knows well what you stand for.
phrases.explanation: The verse then says that Allah knows the state they are in, and the commentary explains this as His knowledge of their obedience or disobedience in this very matter. The phrase covers conduct that nobody else could see, which is why it matters after an instruction about slipping away. Nothing of what people are on, whether open or concealed, is outside His knowledge.

phrases.translation: And ˹on˺ the Day all will be returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did.
phrases.explanation: The next sentence names the day of account. On the Day all will be returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did, and the commentary explains this as making known to them what they sent ahead of disobedience and then repaying them for it. The information is not new to Allah, only to them. The verse completes the movement from a small act at a gathering to a full and public reckoning.

phrases.translation: For Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things
phrases.explanation: The surah ends with the statement that supports everything before it. Allah has perfect knowledge of all things, and the commentary explains this as His knowledge of every deed performed by every person, nothing hidden from Him, and His full recompense for each worker. The chapter that began with a slander nobody thought Allah had heard ends with the assurance that He hears and knows all of it.
